passage: It was past midnight in the hostel, the power had gone out, and Karthik's phone was at nine percent. For three weeks he had swung between missing Sabina and wanting her to hurt. Tonight the anger was winning. He typed a long post about what she had done, with a photo, and his thumb hovered over the share button. Then the screen dimmed and the battery warning flashed. Instead of hunting for a charger to finish it, he saved the draft, muted her chat and knocked on his roommate's door. "Can I sit here? I'm not okay." The roommate handed him a blanket and switched on a torch. Karthik sent nothing. In the morning he asked the roommate to help him stick to not contacting Sabina for a month.

qa.q: What was the battery of Karthik's phone at?
qa.a: It was at nine percent.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling about Sabina that night?
qa.a: He swung between missing her and wanting her to hurt, and that night the anger was winning over the longing.

qa.q: What helped Karthik not send the post?
qa.a: He saved the draft, muted the chat, sat with his roommate and asked for help sticking to a month of no contact.

qa.q: How might Sabina have been affected if the post had been shared?
qa.a: Being shamed in public would probably have hurt and frightened her, so not sharing protected both of them.

grounding: An ex-partner cycles between longing and rage and is tempted to shame the ex online, but chooses no contact and support.

passage:
"Thanks for meeting," said Sarika. "I wanted to say something in person."

"Okay." Irawati stirred her tea. "I'm not angry anymore, you know."

"Good. Neither am I. I wanted to thank you. You taught me to cook properly and to say what I need. I didn't always do that. I'm sorry for the year I went silent."

"I wasn't a saint," said Irawati. "I got jealous about your late nights and I said things I regret."

They laughed a little, uneasily.

"We were good together for a while," said Sarika. "And it's all right that it ended."

"Yes." Irawati smiled, her eyes wet. "Send me a photo of the first dish you cook alone."

At the door they hugged briefly and went their separate ways.

qa.q: What did Sarika thank Irawati for?
qa.a: Sarika thanked Irawati for teaching Sarika to cook properly and to say what is needed.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she asked for a photo of the first dish?
qa.a: She was feeling warm and a little sad; her eyes were wet but she smiled, accepting the ending without turning Sarika into a villain.

qa.q: What does this conversation show about closing a relationship well?
qa.a: Both admitted their part, named what they had learned, and let go without rewriting the relationship as all bad.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when Irawati admitted her own jealousy?
qa.a: Sarika was probably relieved that the fault was shared, and the two of them laughed a little, uneasily, together.

grounding: An ex-partner acknowledges what the relationship taught and lets go without turning it into pure villainy.

passage:
Deepak: hey, are you free at 8 tonight? want to sort out the dishes and the wifi bill. not an angry thing, promise
Mahima: sure. what's up?
Deepak: i've washed the dishes 5 days in a row and the wifi share is due. could we make a chore chart? i'll draw it up
Mahima: fair. exams have flattened me this week. can we do alternate days and i pay the wifi by friday?
Deepak: that works. thank you for hearing me 🙂
Mahima: thanks for asking nicely instead of leaving a note on the fridge 😅
Deepak: haha. see you at 8

qa.q: How many days in a row had Deepak washed the dishes?
qa.a: Deepak had washed the dishes 5 days in a row.

qa.q: Why did Deepak ask to talk at eight and say it was not an angry thing?
qa.a: Deepak wanted a calm moment to sort things out, so that Mahima would not feel attacked.

qa.q: What made the plan easy to agree on?
qa.a: Deepak gave specifics and a proposed fix, and Mahima could add a limit of Mahima's own, alternate days because of exams.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt on seeing the first message?
qa.a: Mahima may have been a little worried at first, but the friendly tone and the promise of no anger made it easy to answer fairly.

grounding: A roommate raises broken agreements at a calm time with specifics and a proposed fix instead of a passive-aggressive note.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage: Asif had a sheet of paper folded in his pocket: a plan for a two-year design course, the fees, and a list of jobs it could lead to. All week he had rehearsed at the dining table, but each time Ammi mentioned the neighbour's son at the engineering college, his words dried up. He felt the weight of his father's overtime too. On Sunday his cousin Karthik said, "If you defy them or just go along, you'll resent both. Show them the plan." That evening Asif put the paper on the table. "Abba, Ammi, I know what you have given up for my studies. I want to try design, and here is how I would pay, and what I would do if it hasn't worked by the end of the first year." His father read it twice. "Ask me again tomorrow," he said. It wasn't yes. But Ammi refilled Asif's plate.

qa.q: What did Asif carry folded in his pocket?
qa.a: He carried a plan for a two-year design course, with the fees and a list of jobs.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as he rehearsed at the dining table?
qa.a: He was torn and guilty; his words dried up because he felt the weight of his father's overtime and the family's expectations.

qa.q: Why did Karthik's advice help?
qa.a: It offered a third route between defying and going along: an honest, respectful conversation with a concrete plan.

qa.q: How might Asif's father have felt while reading the plan?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and worried but respectful of the effort, since he read it twice and asked for a day, which suggests he was taking it seriously.

grounding: A young adult torn between own aspiration and family expectation has an honest, respectful talk with a concrete plan.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage: On the balcony of the flat, Afreen brought two cups of tea to her father, Jagdish, who was sorting bills. "Papa, I want to say thank you. The tuition fees, the extra shifts you took. I wouldn't be here without that." Jagdish waved it off, but he looked pleased. "And," Afreen went on, "I've accepted the internship in another city. I've thought it through and it's my decision. I'll call every Sunday, and I'll tell you if I need help." His smile stiffened. "We thought you would work at the local bank." "I know. I'm grateful you wanted that for me. But I need to try this." Jagdish looked at the bills, then at her. "Send me the address," he said at last.

qa.q: What did Afreen bring to her father on the balcony?
qa.a: She brought two cups of tea to her father, Jagdish.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when his smile stiffened?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and a little worried, since he had hoped Afreen would work at the local bank.

qa.q: What did Afreen do to keep the talk respectful?
qa.a: She thanked him first, explained that the decision was hers, and promised to call every Sunday. 🙂

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when her father said, "Send me the address"?
qa.a: Afreen was probably relieved and grateful, since after his stiff smile it showed he was accepting her decision.

grounding: A young adult thanks parents for their sacrifices while stating boundaries about her own life decisions.

passage: Simran, sit down. You asked why I still practise the breathing but stopped going to the ashram in my second year of college. I am Maria, and at twenty I sat at the feet of a teacher we called Guruji. I was lonely in the city, and the chanting hall made me feel held. His morning talks gave me a calm I had never known. But slowly I noticed things. He asked large donations from people who could barely pay. He told one girl to stop writing to her mother. And his face went cold when anyone asked a question. My peace was real, and so was my unease. I went home for a month and stayed with my own mother. I kept the breathing and the friends. I also kept my questions, and my savings.

qa.q: What did Maria notice about the donations?
qa.a: Guruji asked large donations from people who could barely pay.

qa.q: What did Maria feel in the chanting hall, and what began to trouble Maria?
qa.a: Maria felt held and calm, but became uneasy about the demands for donations, telling a girl to stop writing to her mother, and the cold reaction to questions.

qa.q: What warning signs would you tell Simran to watch for?
qa.a: Demands for money, pressure to cut off from family, and no room for questions.

qa.q: How might the girl who was told to stop writing to her mother have felt?
qa.a: She was probably confused and lonely, since the instruction cut her off from her family.

grounding: An elder recalls finding peace in devotion to a spiritual teacher while noticing signs of exploitation such as money demands, isolation and suppressed questions.

passage: The train was three hours late, and the only free seat in the packed compartment was next to Rehana, whom Jyoti had barely spoken to since the campus debate. "Only someone who hasn't thought about it would oppose the car-free campus," Jyoti said, and heard how it sounded the moment it left her mouth. Rehana replied quietly, "My grandmother uses a wheelchair, and the shuttle takes forty minutes." Jyoti opened her mouth to argue, then made herself say, "So what you want to protect is people who can't walk far. Tell me the strongest version of your case." For two hours they went through it. Jyoti still favoured the plan, but she wrote down a shuttle idea she had never considered. When the train finally moved, they were still arguing, and also sharing a packet of chips.

qa.q: How late was the train?
qa.a: The train was three hours late.

qa.q: What did Jyoti realise when she heard how her sentence sounded?
qa.a: Jyoti realised she had dismissed Rehana as someone who had not thought, which was contempt and not a reason.

qa.q: How did asking for the strongest version of the case help?
qa.a: It let Jyoti learn what Rehana was protecting, find a shuttle idea and sharpen her own thinking, while keeping the friendship.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt on first hearing Jyoti's sentence?
qa.a: Rehana was probably insulted and dismissed, though Rehana answered quietly with a reason about the grandmother.

grounding: An opponent is dismissed with contempt, then the speaker asks for the strongest version of the other case, improving thinking and keeping the friendship.

passage:
Saturday, midnight.

Argued with Yogesh in the canteen about whether the state should fund private schools. He says yes; I say no. Instead of getting louder I asked, "How did you come to that view?" He went quiet, then told me his sister's government school had one teacher for four classes, and their parents saved for years so she could go to a small private one. I had no idea. I still disagree about the policy. But I get why he cares. And I realised we both want children to get a decent education. We disagree about the route.

I felt strangely light walking home. Next time: ask first, argue second.

- Swati

qa.q: What did Swati ask Yogesh?
qa.a: Swati asked, "How did you come to that view?"

qa.q: What did Swati realise about Yogesh's position?
qa.a: Swati realised that Yogesh cares because of his sister's schooling and that both of them want children to get a decent education, and walked home feeling strangely light and at peace.

qa.q: What could Swati do next time?
qa.a: Swati could ask first and argue second, listening for the shared values underneath the disagreement.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt when asked how he came to his view?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and relieved to be heard instead of attacked, since he went quiet and then shared something personal.

grounding: A young adult asks how an opponent came to a view and finds shared values beneath the disagreement.

subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
passage:
Monday. Mohit rang at nine to say he had got the job at the design studio. Divyansh whooped down the phone, and he meant it. Then he sat on the stairs and felt his own pile of rejection emails pressing on his chest.

Thursday. At the celebration dinner Divyansh laughed at Mohit's jokes and hugged him. On the bus home he scrolled through Mohit's photos, set them beside his own year, and felt worse with every swipe.

Sunday. Divyansh said, "I'm happy for you. And it stings for me too. Both are true." Mohit nodded. "Want to go through your portfolio together tomorrow?" Divyansh smiled and said yes.

qa.q: What job did Mohit get?
qa.a: Mohit got the job at the design studio.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling on the stairs after the call?
qa.a: He was happy for Mohit and pained for himself at once, with his own rejection emails pressing on his chest. ❤️

qa.q: What trap did Divyansh fall into on the bus, and what could help?
qa.a: He compared his year with Mohit's timeline, which made him feel worse; accepting both feelings and working on his own next step would help.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt when Divyansh said both were true?
qa.a: Mohit was probably relieved to hear the honest truth and closer to Divyansh, since he offered to go through the portfolio together.

grounding: A friend feels happy for another's success and pained for himself at once; both are true and comparing timelines is the trap.
